title: Amending a Constitution
hook: A constitution has to last — but not freeze. Amendment rules let it change deliberately, usually demanding more agreement than an ordinary law.
key_points: Amendment is the formal process for changing a constitution's text.
It usually needs a higher bar than ordinary law — supermajorities, referendums, or regional approval.
'Rigid' constitutions are hard to amend; 'flexible' ones can change like ordinary legislation.
The high bar protects fundamental rules from momentary majorities but can entrench outdated provisions.
content_html: A constitution sets a society's most basic rules, so it needs to be stable — but no founding document can anticipate everything, and circumstances change. Amendment is the answer: the formal, lawful procedure for altering the constitution's text. Its defining feature is that it is usually harder than passing an ordinary law. Where a normal bill might need a simple majority, an amendment often demands a supermajority, approval in a public referendum, ratification by regional units, or some combination — a deliberately higher bar.
extra_html: This is why constitutions are described as rigid or flexible. A rigid constitution can be changed only through special, demanding procedures, insulating fundamental rules from the shifting preferences of a single legislature or a narrow majority. A flexible constitution can be amended much like ordinary legislation. Encyclopaedia Britannica notes that the choice involves a real trade-off. A high amendment bar protects rights and structures from momentary passions and gives the system durability and predictability. But the same difficulty can entrench provisions that later prove outdated or harmful, since fixing them requires assembling broad, sometimes elusive, agreement. Designing amendment rules is thus a balance between stability and the capacity to reform.

related.title: What a Constitution Is
related.hook: The rulebook above the rules: a constitution sets out how a government is structured and the limits on its power.

related.title: How a Bill Becomes a Law
related.hook: An idea becomes binding law only after a journey: drafting, committee review, debate, votes, and final approval.

related.title: The Rule of Law
related.hook: The principle that everyone — including those in power — is bound by the same publicly known laws, applied equally.

flashcards.prompt: Why do constitutions usually set a higher bar for amendment than for ordinary laws?
flashcards.back_html: To protect fundamental rules from being changed by a momentary or narrow majority — amendment typically needs supermajorities, referendums, or regional approval.

choices.text: One that is deliberately hard to amend, needing special procedures
One that can never be changed under any circumstances
One that changes automatically every year

flashcards.explanation_html: A rigid constitution requires special, demanding procedures to change; a flexible one can be amended much like ordinary legislation.

flashcards.prompt: What is a downside of making a constitution very hard to amend?

choices.text: Outdated or flawed provisions can become entrenched and hard to fix
It makes ordinary laws impossible to pass
It forces elections to be held more often

flashcards.explanation_html: A high bar guards stability but can lock in provisions that later prove outdated, since reform requires broad agreement.
